flashcards.front: Compare Indonesia's performance on SDG 14 and SDG 15.
flashcards.back: Both represent natural capital and biodiversity. SDG 15 (land ecosystems) is consistently declining; SDG 14 (marine ecosystems) is improving and was a focus of the 2017 and 2025 VNRs. This mixed picture motivates IBSAP 2025–2045. Globally about 30% of SDG 14 and 25% of SDG 15 targets were on track (2023).

flashcards.front: What is IBSAP 2025–2045: mission, functions, alignment?
flashcards.back: Indonesia's biodiversity master plan. Mission: protection, sustainable use, enrichment of science and technology (STI), strengthening resources and governance. Functions: national and regional guideline, diplomatic tool in global forums, evaluated every 5 years. Aligned with RPJPN, KM-GBF; mandated by Presidential Instruction 1/2023.

flashcards.front: Define Nature-based Solutions (NbS) per UNEP and IUCN.
flashcards.back: UNEP: actions to protect, conserve, restore, sustainably use and manage natural or modified ecosystems to address social, economic and environmental challenges. IUCN: solutions benefiting people and nature at once. Address climate, food and water security, disaster risk and urban development; a cost-effective route to the SDGs.

flashcards.front: Define Science, Technology and Innovation (STI) as three related areas.
flashcards.back: Science: pursuit of knowledge through systematic study of the physical, natural and social world. Technology: application of knowledge to achieve specific goals. Innovation: a new way of producing, distributing or using goods and services, based on new technology, new business models or new economic or social organisation (not only technological).

flashcards.front: What does the Addis Ababa Action Agenda say about STI?
flashcards.back: The AAAA (2015) is the UN financing and means-of-implementation framework for the 2030 Agenda. STI is one of its Seven Key Actions. Creating and spreading innovations and technologies, including mutually agreed technology transfer, promotes sustainable development, so every country can steer targets toward universal achievement.

flashcards.front: List the four components of the Technology Facilitation Mechanism (TFM) and group them.
flashcards.back: Internal UN bodies monitoring STI in the SDGs: IATT (UN Interagency Task Team) and the 10-Member Group. Communication and knowledge-exchange platforms: the STI Forum (annual multi-stakeholder forum) and 2030 Connect (online platform and information gateway).

flashcards.front: List the three features of STI for SDG achievement.
flashcards.back: 1) Knowledge-centred: generating, disseminating and using knowledge. 2) Goal-specific: each SDG needs different STI (e.g. vaccines for health, renewables for energy). 3) Place-based Priority: each country needs different STI according to its priorities and local context. No one-size-fits-all.

flashcards.front: What did the UN 2023 midpoint reality check find (numbers)?
flashcards.back: Of 140 targets evaluated: 15% progressing per roadmap, 48% not on track, more than 30% stagnant or regressing below the 2015 baseline. Positives: more databases comparable across countries and more agreed methods. Highest on-track share: SDG 12 (~36%). Climate hampers water and energy progress (SDG 6, 7, 11, 13, 14, 15).

flashcards.front: Give gains and lags from the 2026 reality check.
flashcards.back: Gains: 1 billion gained drinking water, 1.2 billion safe sanitation, HIV infections down 30%, electricity 92%, internet 74%, social protection half the world. Lags: 1 in 10 in extreme poverty, 3 billion food insecure, 1.43°C warming by 2025, 273 million children out of school, refugees up by over half. Gaps persist in SDG 1, 5, 10.

flashcards.front: Define climate change and name the main components of the climate system.
flashcards.back: Climate change = long-term change in the average atmospheric conditions shaping local, regional and global climate. Past natural drivers: volcanoes, solar radiation, tectonic shifts, orbital changes. Today's change is extraordinarily fast and primarily human-driven. Climate system components (IPCC 2021): atmosphere, biosphere, cryosphere, oceans.

flashcards.front: What are GHGs, and why are they both essential and a problem?
flashcards.back: Gases that absorb heat energy emitted from Earth's surface (<1% of air molecules). Natural greenhouse effect keeps average surface temperature above freezing, so life can exist. Natural: water vapor, CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, ozone. Industrial: CFCs, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆. Excess human emissions enhance the effect and cause global warming.

flashcards.front: What do the GHG concentration data show, and which numbers matter?
flashcards.back: Ice cores (800,000 years): CO₂ stayed roughly 180–300 ppm, then rose sharply after the Industrial Revolution (~1760). CO₂ = 409.9 ppm in 2019 (IPCC); NOAA 2023: CO₂ 419.3 ppm (+50%), CH₄ 1922.6 ppb (+166%), N₂O 336.7 ppb (+25%). CO₂ in ppm, methane in ppb.

flashcards.front: Explain the enhanced greenhouse effect and GWP. Which protocol covers which gases?
flashcards.back: Extra human CO₂/CH₄ enhance the greenhouse effect, so average temperature rises: global warming. GWP = heat a gas traps over a period relative to CO₂ (GWP = 1); N₂O ≈ 298. Kyoto regulates 6 GHGs (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFC, PFC, SF₆). Montreal Protocol covers CFCs (GWP up to ~12,500) and HCFCs (HCFC-22 ≈ 1,800).

flashcards.front: Which gases are GHGs and which are not?
flashcards.back: GHGs: water vapor (H₂O), CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, ozone (O₃); industrial CFCs/HCFCs, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆. NOT GHGs: ammonia (NH₃) and the bulk gases nitrogen (N₂) and oxygen (O₂). Each GHG has a Global Warming Potential (GWP).

flashcards.front: Why can climate change make the SDGs hard to achieve?
flashcards.back: IOC and WMO: climate change can hinder or reverse progress on other SDGs. Weather, climate and water impacts cause slow-onset and fast-onset disasters: temperature rise, sea-level rise, and disruption of land and sea ecosystems. Reality-check framing: SDG 6, 7, 11, 13, 14, 15 are hit. Cambridge (2024) barriers: finance (~48%), greenwashing, marginalised state, top-down intervention, misguided scaling of social enterprise.

flashcards.front: How does SDG 13 (climate) affect the other SDGs, and who is most vulnerable?
flashcards.back: Extreme weather events cause setbacks across health, food, water, cities and livelihoods. COVID-19 cut global GHG emissions by about 6%. Most vulnerable: Small Island Developing States (SIDS), coastal areas, Global South countries, and women, children, youth and other marginalised groups.

flashcards.front: Give examples of how other SDGs contribute to SDG 13.
flashcards.back: SDG 7: renewable transition cuts GHGs. SDG 11: green transport, efficiency, green planning. SDG 12: waste management, less overconsumption, circular economy. SDG 14 & 15: restoring forests, mangroves, marine ecosystems for carbon sequestration. SDG 2: agroforestry, organic fertiliser. About half of emissions stay in the atmosphere; the rest is absorbed by land and oceans.

flashcards.front: Compare the Paris Agreement (2015) with the Kyoto Protocol (1997), and state Paris's goals.
flashcards.back: Kyoto: top-down targets, developing countries not committed, USA did not join. Paris: all countries set own targets (NDCs). Goals: (1) mitigation, well below 2°C, pursue 1.5°C; (2) adaptation and resilience; (3) align finance flows with low-emission, climate-resilient development. Principles: equity, transparency, sovereignty.

flashcards.front: List the three principles of the Paris Agreement and their mechanisms.
flashcards.back: Equity: CBDR-RC. Transparency: Global Stocktake (GST). Sovereignty: bottom-up architecture with NDCs, each country determines its own level of emissions and reports it as an NDC (its pledge).

flashcards.front: What does CBDR-RC stand for and what does each part mean?
flashcards.back: Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (equity principle; negotiation term 'Right to Development'). Common: all countries contribute to climate change, to varying degrees. Differentiated: 'ability to pay', developed countries commit more. Respective capabilities: support via TFM and funding so all can participate.

flashcards.front: What is the Global Stocktake (GST), which principle does it represent, and what is its aim?
flashcards.back: GST = transparency principle. It assesses how far countries implement their climate commitments (reviews progress) to continually raise ambition and avoid an emergency, e.g. less fossil fuel, more renewables, more climate funding. COP24 added loss and damage and response measures; first GST concluded at COP28 (2023).

flashcards.front: What is Indonesia's climate commitment under Paris?
flashcards.back: Paris ratified as Law No. 16/2016. Keep temperature rise <1.5°C. Net Zero Emission (NZE) by 2060 or earlier. Emission cut targets are split into unconditional (independent) and conditional (with international support); slide 19 lists 29% / 41% for 2030, later updated to 31.89% / 43.2%.

flashcards.front: What numbers does the quiz attach to Indonesia's Enhanced NDC, and what do conditional vs unconditional mean?
flashcards.back: Quiz answer: 31.89% GHG reduction independently (unconditional, domestic effort) and 43.2% with international support (conditional). Slide 19 shows the first NDC as 29% / 41%, and slide 20 shows 31.89% / 43.20% as the 2035 target of the Second NDC, so learn the numbers firmly. Conditional targets depend on finance and technology.

flashcards.front: What is Indonesia's Second NDC (2025) and what are its scenarios?
flashcards.back: Responds to the 1st Global Stocktake. 2035 absolute emission reduction targets: 31.89% unconditional and 43.20% conditional; shift from relative to absolute targets; NZE 2060 or sooner. Scenarios: CPOS (Current Policy), LCCP_Low and LCCP_High (Low Carbon Compatible with Paris).

flashcards.front: What did the 2023 urban heat events in Indonesia show, and what are the impacts?
flashcards.back: BMKG said it was not technically a heat wave, yet the highest temperatures on record (2023) were in Semarang, Surabaya and Makassar. Impacts: heat strain, heat stress, psychosocial disorders and disrupted cognitive performance. Effects differ by socio-economic status.

flashcards.front: Why is air conditioning both an adaptation tool and a risk?
flashcards.back: Adaptation: life-saving in extreme heat, especially for vulnerable groups; maintains quality of life and work productivity. Risk: high energy use and release of HFC refrigerants increase GHGs. Result: potential maladaptation (a vicious cycle), hence the need for sustainable cooling.

flashcards.front: Distinguish direct and indirect emissions from cooling systems.
flashcards.back: Direct: high-GWP refrigerants (CFC, HCFC, HFC) leaking from units or mishandled during servicing. Indirect: energy consumed by cooling, which can reach 50–60% of total energy use in hotels, offices and shopping centres. Measured in CO₂e.

flashcards.front: List the five principles of sustainable cooling.
flashcards.back: (1) Energy savings (efficient equipment, passive design); (2) environmentally friendly refrigerants (zero ODP, low GWP); (3) integration of renewable energy (solar-powered cooling); (4) fair and affordable access (cold storage for traditional fishermen, village cooperatives); (5) circular economy and end-of-life management.

flashcards.front: What does the energy-savings principle of sustainable cooling include?
flashcards.back: Use energy-efficient ACs, refrigerators, freezers, cold storage and chillers, and reduce the thermal load by passive design: effective ventilation, insulation and shading. It targets indirect (energy) emissions.

flashcards.front: What two criteria must a sustainable-cooling refrigerant meet?
flashcards.back: Zero ODP (Ozone Depleting Potential, does not damage the ozone layer) and low GWP (does not contribute to global warming). Problem gases: CFCs, HCFCs and HFCs, whose leakage and servicing cause high direct emissions.

flashcards.front: What is the renewable-energy principle of sustainable cooling?
flashcards.back: Integrate renewable energy into cooling, the named example being solar-powered cooling systems. This lowers indirect emissions from the electricity that cooling consumes.

flashcards.front: What does circular economy and end-of-life management mean for cooling?
flashcards.back: Manage used refrigerants so they are not released directly into the air, and recycle cooling units at end-of-life. Prevents high-GWP CFC/HCFC/HFC leakage after use.

flashcards.front: Rank global GHG emissions by sector in 2019 with their shares.
flashcards.back: Energy 34% (20 GtCO₂-eq) > Industry 24% (14) > AFOLU 22% (13) > Transportation 15% (8.7) > Buildings 6% (3.3). Source: IPCC 2023. About half of AFOLU net emissions are CO₂ from LULUCF, mainly deforestation.

flashcards.front: Define carbon sequestration and give its three types.
flashcards.back: Natural or artificial processes by which CO₂ is removed from the atmosphere or diverted from emission sources, then stored in oceans, terrestrial environments (vegetation, soil, sediments) and geological formations. Types: biological, geological (injected in porous rock), technological (e.g. Direct Air Capture, USD 500–800 per tonne).

flashcards.front: Why do tropical peatlands matter for climate, and how do they form?
flashcards.back: Peatlands cover about 3% of land but store twice as much carbon as all forests. They form where waterlogging limits oxygen so production exceeds decomposition (average depth 5.5–7 m, up to 20 m). A high water table is the key control on decomposition; keeping peat wet is the key lever.

flashcards.front: How does disturbance turn Indonesian peatlands into CO₂ sources?
flashcards.back: Fire, drainage and deforestation release CO₂. Drainage lowers the water table, upper peat turns aerobic, giving 'cold fire': steady CO₂ emission. Dry-season fires (El Niño) give occasional but extensive emissions. Borneo: 26.63 Mha (47.72%) of 55.81 Mha forest logged by 2010.

flashcards.front: What are the AFOLU mitigation strategies, and what is not one?
flashcards.back: AFOLU = Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (22% of 2019 emissions). Strategies: afforestation, reforestation and forest ecosystem restoration; agroforestry; soil carbon management; bioenergy in agriculture. Land clearing by burning is NOT mitigation (it is an emission source).

flashcards.front: What is an SDG spillover? Give an example.
flashcards.back: Effect of a country's policies, practices or trade on other countries' SDG progress; a country can raise its own score while pushing harm abroad. Measured with a footprint approach. Example: importing rice (target 2.1) causes biodiversity loss in the exporter (15.5); palm oil drives deforestation and poor labour conditions (SDG 8).

flashcards.front: What principles underlie SDG interlinkages, and why do rankings mislead?
flashcards.back: SDGs are not achieved one by one; the 2030 Agenda rests on being transformative, universal and indivisible, grounded in systems thinking. Interlinkages show how progress on one target affects others; implementation must be coherent and context-specific. Rankings and linear correlations ignore interlinkages, local context, No One Left Behind and spillovers.

flashcards.front: Define synergy and trade-off between SDGs, with examples.
flashcards.back: Synergy (reinforcing): action gives positive change in both objectives, e.g. clean energy (SDG 7) helping education (4) and health (3). Trade-off (counteracting): positive change in one comes with negative change in another, e.g. agriculture (SDG 2) driving deforestation (15) and water use (6). Aim: maximise synergies, minimise trade-offs.

flashcards.front: List the four activity types and the matching strategy for each.
flashcards.back: Core (synergy; many positive, few negative): scale positive impact. Mixed (significant positive and negative): decouple negatives. Opposed (mainly negative, e.g. coal mining, alcohol, tobacco): transform. Peripheral (insignificant, e.g. cultural preservation): explore ways to add positive impact.

flashcards.front: What are mixed activities? Give the two slide examples.
flashcards.back: Activities with both significant positive and negative SDG impacts. Large-scale agricultural expansion (SDG 2): feeds people but drives deforestation (15), is the largest freshwater user (6), and can widen inequality (10). Renewable energy (SDG 7): energy access but long-term trade-offs such as bird deaths, marine habitat loss, loss of fertile land (SDG 14/15).

flashcards.front: Why can recycling cost more than new material, and what is single vs dual stream?
flashcards.back: Collecting, sorting and cleaning mixed waste is costly. Since 2018 China rejects recyclables below 99% purity (Indonesia and African countries also receive them). Single stream: one container, mixed material qualities. Dual stream: sorted by quality, raising market value. Trade-off: collection convenience vs processing cost and quality.

flashcards.front: How does technology use affect SDG 12, and what does the inverted-U curve show?
flashcards.back: Development and technology use raise material and environmental footprints, hindering SDG 12 (targets 12.2 and 8.4). Inverted-U: per capita material footprint rises with per capita income until a turning point, then falls (decoupling). Examples: IKN construction materials, 12 coal power plants. This is the T of IPAT.

flashcards.front: Compare SDG synergies in the Global North and South (Boar et al. 2021).
flashcards.back: Global North: synergies include all three dimensions (social, economic, environmental); new technology and renewable energy reduce environmental impact. Global South: synergies cover only one dimension, so gains in one area often come at others' expense. North's synergies may partly rely on outsourcing impacts through spillovers.

flashcards.front: Define the nexus approach and its principles.
flashcards.back: Deepens integration between goals and targets across sectors, avoids unsustainable and inefficient conflicts and overlaps, and strengthens synergies while reducing trade-offs. Principles: ensure access to resources for vulnerable groups, promote efficient use of resources, ensure sustainability. Countries prioritise SDGs by local context.

flashcards.front: What is the Food–Energy–Water nexus and which SDGs sit at its core?
flashcards.back: Food, energy and water interact and affect the SDGs yet are often managed separately: food needs water and energy, energy needs water and land, water needs energy. Inner ring of the SDG wheel: SDG 2 (food), 6 (water), 7 (energy); managing it well ripples to all 17 SDGs.

flashcards.front: Name and group the nine reasons for a FEW nexus approach.
flashcards.back: A. Basic needs/scarcity: limited access, increasing demand, limited resources. B. Global/environmental: global goods (traded internationally), regional differences, interdependence with climate and environmental change. C. Security/governance: security (a crisis causes instability), tightly regulated markets, identification and management of risks.
